subject: selective
title: Reading comprehension · Test 2
summary: A 30-minute practice reading test with four original passages (including a poem) and 30 multiple-choice questions on main idea, inference, vocabulary, tone and poetry.
body:
Read the four passages below, then answer the 30 questions. You have 30 minutes. Each question names the passage it is about. Passage D is a poster, described in words. Look back at the passage for every answer — the evidence is always there in the text.

## Passage A — The Spare Key

Sam had been avoiding Mrs Okafor for two months, ever since his football had gone through her front window.

He had paid for the glass out of his birthday money, and she had said, "Accidents happen," in a voice that made it sound as if they didn't. Since then he had crossed the street whenever he saw her watering her roses. He had become an expert on the exact timing of her mornings.

So when he came home on the hottest afternoon of the year and found his pocket empty — no key, just a hole in the lining — his first feeling was not panic. It was dread. Mum would not be home until seven. His phone was on two per cent. And the only other person on Banksia Street with a spare key to his house was Mrs Okafor.

He sat on the front step for twenty minutes, telling himself it wasn't that hot. A magpie watched him from the fence with what looked like pity. The concrete burned through his shorts.

At last he trudged next door and knocked, very softly, in the hope that she would not hear.

She opened the door before he had finished knocking. "Sam," she said. "You look like a boiled prawn. Inside."

Her kitchen was cool and smelled of oranges. She poured him a glass of water, then another, and found the key in a drawer full of rubber bands and old birthday candles. She did not mention the window.

"I've seen you crossing the road," she said instead, as she handed him the key. "You don't have to. I was cross about the glass for about a day. Then I remembered that my brother once put a cricket ball through our school principal's windscreen."

Sam didn't know what to say. "What happened to him?"

"He became a principal himself," she said, and laughed so hard she had to hold on to the bench.

The next morning, Sam left for school at his normal time. Mrs Okafor was watering her roses. He did not cross the road. He waved, and she swung the hose in his direction — not quite close enough to hit him.

## Passage B — The Pull of the Moon

If you have ever built a sandcastle near the water and come back to find it gone, you have met the tide. Along most coasts, the sea creeps up the beach and slides away again twice a day. The main cause is not the wind or the weather. It is the Moon.

Every object with mass pulls on every other object. This pull is called gravity. The Moon is much smaller than Earth, but it is close enough for its gravity to tug noticeably on our oceans. The water on the side of Earth facing the Moon is pulled towards it and piles up into a bulge.

Strangely, there is a second bulge on the opposite side of Earth, facing away from the Moon. This happens because the Moon's pull gets weaker with distance. It tugs hardest on the near-side water, a little less on the middle of Earth, and least of all on the far-side water, which is effectively left behind. The result is two bulges of water, one on each side of the planet.

As Earth spins, a beach passes through both bulges, giving most coasts two high tides and two low tides each day. Because the Moon is also moving along its orbit, the timetable slips by about fifty minutes every day, which is why high tide is never at the same time two days running.

The Sun affects the tides too, though less strongly, because it is so far away. When the Sun, Moon and Earth line up — at new moon and full moon — their pulls combine to make extra-high high tides and extra-low low tides. These are called spring tides, a name that has nothing to do with the season. When the Moon looks like a half circle, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles, and the difference between high and low tide is smallest. These gentler tides are called neap tides.

The shape of the coast matters as well. In wide, funnel-shaped bays, the incoming water is squeezed together and rises much higher. Parts of the Kimberley coast in Western Australia have some of the biggest tides in the country, with the sea rising and falling by more than ten metres.

So the next time your sandcastle disappears, you can blame something nearly 400,000 kilometres away.

## Passage C — The Shed

My grandfather's shed  
smells of oil and sawdust and something older,  
like rain kept in a tin.

Jars of screws line the shelves,  
sorted by size, by shine, by a system  
only he understood.  
Each one is labelled in his careful capitals,  
the ink gone brown as tea.

He never threw anything away.  
"That might be useful," he would say,  
holding up a bent hinge, a single glove,  
a key to a lock that no longer existed.

Now the bench is bare  
except for his reading glasses,  
folded, waiting,  
as if he has just stepped out  
to look at the weather.

I pick up a jar and shake it.  
The screws rattle like small applause.  
I put it back exactly where it was.

## Passage D — Poster: Planting Day

*This poster is pinned up in a local library. It is described in words below.*

The top third of the poster shows two photographs side by side. The left photograph shows a bare, dusty creek bank. The right photograph shows the same creek bank covered in young green trees. A thick white arrow points from the left photograph to the right one. Above the photographs, in large green capital letters, is the headline:

**ONE MORNING. ONE HUNDRED TREES. ONE CREEK REBORN.**

Below the photographs, in smaller black writing:

Join your neighbours at the Wattle Gully Planting Day!
Saturday, 8:30 am to 12 noon
Meet at the Wattle Gully Reserve car park, Hill Street

- Gloves, tools and morning tea provided
- Wear closed shoes and a hat
- Children welcome with an adult
- No experience needed — we'll show you how

In the bottom right-hand corner, inside a bright yellow circle that is tilted at an angle, are the words: **Free sausage sizzle for every planter!**

Along the very bottom, in small grey writing: *Run by the Friends of Wattle Gully. Bookings are not essential, but they help us order enough trees. Book at the library front desk.*

questions.prompt: In Passage A, Sam's 'first feeling was not panic. It was dread.' Here 'dread' means

options.A: great excitement about what comes next
options.B: deep tiredness after a long day
options.C: anger at someone who has let him down
options.D: a heavy fear of something unpleasant that is about to happen

questions.explanation: Sam dreads having to ask Mrs Okafor for the key — he fears an unpleasant meeting that is coming. The heat might suggest tiredness, but dread is about what lies ahead.
steps: Find what Sam must do next: ask Mrs Okafor, the person he has avoided for two months.
His feeling is about something unpleasant he cannot escape.
So 'dread' means a heavy fear of something about to happen.

mistakes.A: Trap: missing the mood. Sam is locked out and must face someone he has been avoiding — nothing exciting.
mistakes.B: Trap: guessing from the heat. 'Dread' is a feeling about what is coming, not tiredness.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing the wrong feeling. Sam is not angry at anyone; he is worried about having to visit Mrs Okafor.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, why had Sam been crossing the street whenever he saw Mrs Okafor?

options.A: She had told him to stay away from her house.
options.B: He still owed her money for the glass.
options.C: He felt awkward and embarrassed about breaking her window.
options.D: He was trying to avoid the magpie on her fence.

questions.explanation: The avoiding started 'ever since his football had gone through her front window', and her cool 'Accidents happen' made him feel worse — so he felt awkward. He had already paid for the glass, so he did not owe money.
steps: Find when the avoiding started: 'ever since his football had gone through her front window.'
He had already paid, but her tone made him feel she was still upset.
So he crossed the road because he felt awkward and embarrassed.

mistakes.A: Trap: inventing a reason. She never said this — later she tells him he doesn't have to cross the road.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing a detail. The passage says he had already paid with his birthday money.
mistakes.D: Trap: grabbing a nearby detail. The magpie only appears later, while Sam waits on his own front step, and has nothing to do with his avoiding her.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, Mrs Okafor says Sam looks 'like a boiled prawn'. This tells us Sam was

options.A: hungry and hoping for food
options.B: pale and frightened
options.C: sunburnt after a day at the beach
options.D: red-faced and overheated from sitting in the sun

questions.explanation: Boiled prawns turn bright pink-red, and Sam has sat on hot concrete on the hottest afternoon of the year — he is red and overheated. The beach option adds a place that isn't in the story.
steps: Picture a boiled prawn: bright pink-red.
Sam has just sat on burning concrete on the hottest afternoon of the year.
So the simile shows he is red-faced and overheated.

mistakes.A: Trap: thinking of prawns as food. The comparison is about how he looks, not what he wants.
mistakes.B: Trap: ignoring the colour. Boiled prawns are bright pink-red, not pale.
mistakes.C: Trap: adding details. He has been sitting on his front step, not at the beach.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, why does Sam knock 'very softly'?

options.A: He does not want to wake her from a nap.
options.B: His hands are burnt from the hot concrete.
options.C: He thinks the door is made of glass.
options.D: Part of him hopes he can avoid facing Mrs Okafor.

questions.explanation: The sentence says he knocked softly 'in the hope that she would not hear' — he still wants to avoid her. A nap is never mentioned.
steps: Read the whole sentence: he knocked very softly 'in the hope that she would not hear.'
Why would he hope that? He has been avoiding her for two months.
So he knocks softly because part of him hopes to avoid facing her.

mistakes.A: Trap: a sensible guess that ignores the text. The writer tells us the reason: 'in the hope that she would not hear'.
mistakes.B: Trap: twisting a detail. The concrete burned through his shorts, not his hands.
mistakes.C: Trap: confusing details. The broken glass was her front window, and nothing says the door is glass.

questions.prompt: In Passage A, what does Mrs Okafor's story about her brother mainly show?

options.A: She sees the broken window as an ordinary mistake that does not define a person.
options.B: Her family has always disliked school principals.
options.C: She expects Sam to cause more damage soon.
options.D: Her brother is still upset, many years later, about breaking the principal's windscreen.

questions.explanation: Her brother broke a principal's windscreen yet grew up to become a principal — so one accident doesn't decide who you are. She tells Sam this right after saying he doesn't need to avoid her.
steps: Note when she tells the story: right after 'You don't have to' cross the road.
The story: her brother broke a principal's windscreen, then became a principal himself.
So she is showing that a mistake like Sam's is ordinary and doesn't define him.

mistakes.B: Trap: missing the point of the joke. Her brother went on to become a principal himself.
mistakes.C: Trap: misreading her purpose. She tells the story to make Sam feel better, not to warn him.
mistakes.D: Trap: confusing who was upset. The story is about her brother breaking a windscreen, then doing well in life.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes how Mrs Okafor speaks when she opens the door in Passage A?

options.A: Cold and unwelcoming
options.B: Brisk but kind
options.C: Nervous and unsure
options.D: Mocking and cruel

questions.explanation: 'Sam. You look like a boiled prawn. Inside.' is short and bossy (brisk), but she brings him into the cool and gives him water (kind). Short sentences can seem cold, but her actions show care.
steps: Look at her words: short, direct commands — 'Inside.'
Look at her actions: she brings him into the cool, gives him two glasses of water and the key.
So she is brisk but kind.

mistakes.A: Trap: judging by length only. Her words are short, but she calls him in, gives him water and finds the key.
mistakes.C: Trap: no evidence. She opens the door at once and takes charge.
mistakes.D: Trap: taking the prawn joke the wrong way. She teases, but her actions are caring.

questions.prompt: Which title would best suit the main idea of Passage A?

options.A: Mending More Than Glass
options.B: The Hottest Day of the Year
options.C: How to Hide a Spare Key
options.D: A Magpie's Pity

questions.explanation: The story is about Sam and Mrs Okafor repairing their relationship after the broken window — 'more than glass'. The heat is only the setting.
steps: Ask: what changes from the start to the end? Sam stops avoiding Mrs Okafor and they become friendly.
The window glass was already fixed; what gets repaired in the story is their relationship.
So 'Mending More Than Glass' fits the main idea best.

mistakes.B: Trap: choosing the setting. The heat is the background, not what the story is about.
mistakes.C: Trap: choosing a small detail. The key gets Sam to the door; the story is about him and Mrs Okafor.
mistakes.D: Trap: choosing a one-line detail. The magpie appears in a single sentence.

questions.prompt: At the end of Passage A, Mrs Okafor swings the hose towards Sam, 'not quite close enough to hit him'. This most likely suggests that

options.A: she is still secretly angry about the window
options.B: she did not notice him and it was an accident
options.C: she is teasing him in a friendly way, showing they are now on good terms
options.D: she is trying to cool him down because he looks hot again

questions.explanation: Sam waves, and she answers with a playful gesture that deliberately misses — a joke between neighbours who are now relaxed together. Anger doesn't fit: she has said she was cross 'for about a day'.
steps: Sam waves instead of crossing the road — he is no longer avoiding her.
She swings the hose his way but deliberately not close enough to hit him: a joke.
So it suggests friendly teasing — they are now on good terms.

mistakes.A: Trap: ignoring 'not quite close enough'. She chooses not to wet him, and she has just said she was cross for only a day.
mistakes.B: Trap: missing the wave. Sam waves to her, and she responds by swinging the hose his way.
mistakes.D: Trap: copying yesterday's detail. It is morning and she deliberately misses him — it's a joke, not help.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Passage B, 'The Pull of the Moon'?

options.A: To warn people not to build sandcastles near the sea
options.B: To argue that the Sun matters more than the Moon for tides
options.C: To explain what causes tides and why they change
options.D: To describe a holiday on the Kimberley coast

questions.explanation: The passage explains gravity, the two bulges, daily timing, spring and neap tides, and coastline shape — all causes and changes of tides. It says the Sun matters less, so it does not argue the opposite.
steps: List what the paragraphs cover: gravity, two bulges, timing, spring and neap tides, coast shape.
All of these explain how tides work and why they vary.
So the purpose is to explain what causes tides and why they change.

mistakes.A: Trap: taking the opening example as the purpose. The sandcastle just introduces the topic.
mistakes.B: Trap: reversing a fact. The passage says the Sun's effect is less strong.
mistakes.D: Trap: choosing one detail. The Kimberley is a single example of big tides.

questions.prompt: According to Passage B, spring tides happen when

options.A: it is the season of spring
options.B: the Sun and Moon pull at right angles
options.C: strong winds blow towards the shore
options.D: the Sun, Moon and Earth line up

questions.explanation: The passage says when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up 'these are called spring tides'. The season is ruled out directly.
steps: Find 'spring tides' in the passage.
The sentence before says: when the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, their pulls combine.
So spring tides happen when the three line up.

mistakes.A: Trap: trusting the name. The passage says the name 'has nothing to do with the season'.
mistakes.B: Trap: mixing up the two kinds. Right angles give neap tides.
mistakes.C: Trap: ignoring the passage. It says the cause is 'not the wind or the weather'.

questions.prompt: Using Passage B, if high tide at a beach is at 9:00 am on Monday, when would you expect the morning high tide on Tuesday?

options.A: About 9:50 am
options.B: About 9:00 am
options.C: About 8:10 am
options.D: About 9:00 pm

questions.explanation: The tides slip about fifty minutes later each day: 9:00 am + 50 min = 9:50 am. Choosing 9:00 am ignores the line 'never at the same time two days running'.
steps: Find the timing fact: the timetable 'slips by about fifty minutes every day'.
Add 50 minutes to 9:00 am.

mistakes.B: Trap: ignoring the slip. The passage says the timetable slips by about fifty minutes every day.
mistakes.C: Trap: moving the wrong way. The tide 'slips' later each day, so add the fifty minutes.
mistakes.D: Trap: confusing which tide. The question asks for Tuesday morning's high tide, and 9:00 pm is not a day later.

questions.prompt: In Passage B, the far-side water 'is effectively left behind'. Here 'effectively' means

options.A: skilfully and successfully
options.B: as good as, in practice
options.C: very quickly
options.D: on purpose

questions.explanation: The far-side water is not really left behind — it is pulled a little — but it acts as if it were. 'Effectively' means 'in practice' here. 'Skilfully' is the everyday meaning and does not fit water.
steps: The Moon still pulls the far-side water, just the least.
So the water is not truly left behind; it behaves as if it were.
'Effectively' here means 'as good as' or 'in practice'.

mistakes.A: Trap: the usual meaning of 'effective'. Water cannot do something skilfully; here it means 'in effect'.
mistakes.C: Trap: guessing from the movement. Speed is not discussed in this sentence.
mistakes.D: Trap: giving water a will. The water is not choosing to stay behind.

questions.prompt: According to Passage B, why is there a high tide on the side of Earth facing away from the Moon?

options.A: The Moon pulls the far-side water less than the rest of Earth, so that water is left behind as a bulge.
options.B: The Sun pulls that water towards it.
options.C: The Moon's pull is strongest on the far side of Earth, so the water there is dragged outwards the furthest.
options.D: The water is pushed there by winds from the near side.

questions.explanation: The Moon pulls hardest on near water, less on Earth's middle and least on far water, which is 'left behind' as a bulge. Saying the pull is strongest on the far side reverses the passage.
steps: Find the paragraph about the second bulge.
The pull weakens with distance: strongest near, weaker in the middle, weakest far.
So the far-side water is left behind as a bulge.

mistakes.B: Trap: bringing in the wrong body. The Sun does not cause the second bulge in the passage's explanation.
mistakes.C: Trap: reversing the rule. The passage says the pull weakens with distance, so it is weakest on the far side.
mistakes.D: Trap: ignoring the opening. The passage rules out wind as the cause of tides.

questions.prompt: A student goes to the beach on the day of a full moon. Based on Passage B, what should she expect?

options.A: A bigger difference than usual between high and low tide
options.B: Only one high tide that day
options.C: The smallest difference between high and low tide
options.D: No tides at all because the Moon is full

questions.explanation: At full moon the Sun, Moon and Earth line up, giving spring tides — extra-high highs and extra-low lows, so a bigger range. The 'smallest difference' option describes neap tides.
steps: Full moon means the Sun, Moon and Earth line up.
Lining up gives spring tides: extra-high high tides and extra-low low tides.
So she should expect a bigger difference than usual between high and low tide.

mistakes.B: Trap: forgetting the two bulges. Most coasts get two high tides every day.
mistakes.C: Trap: mixing up spring and neap tides. The smallest difference comes when the Moon looks like a half circle.
mistakes.D: Trap: misreading. A full moon makes tides bigger, not stop.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer of Passage B begin and end with a sandcastle?

options.A: Because the passage is mainly about building sandcastles
options.B: To argue that sandcastles damage beaches
options.C: To connect the science to a familiar experience and round off the text neatly
options.D: To prove to readers, using the sandcastle, that the Moon is nearly 400,000 kilometres away

questions.explanation: Starting and ending with a disappearing sandcastle hooks readers with something they know and makes the ending link back to the start. The passage itself is about tides, not sandcastles.
steps: Notice where the sandcastle appears: only the first and last paragraphs.
Everything in between explains tides; the sandcastle is an everyday example readers recognise.
So it links the science to familiar experience and neatly frames the text.

mistakes.A: Trap: mistaking the frame for the topic. The middle paragraphs are all about tides.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing an argument. Nothing in the passage blames sandcastles for anything.
mistakes.D: Trap: misreading the last line. The distance is mentioned for effect, not proved.

questions.prompt: Beach P is on a straight, open coast. Beach Q is at the narrow end of a wide, funnel-shaped bay nearby. Which statement is best supported by Passage B?

options.A: Beach P will have bigger tides because it faces the open ocean.
options.B: Both beaches will have exactly the same tides because the Moon is equally far away.
options.C: Beach Q will usually have a bigger tidal range than Beach P.
options.D: Beach Q will have no low tide because the water is trapped.

questions.explanation: The passage says water in wide, funnel-shaped bays is 'squeezed together and rises much higher', so Beach Q should have bigger tides. 'Exactly the same' ignores that coast shape matters.
steps: Find what the passage says about coast shape: funnel-shaped bays squeeze incoming water so it rises much higher.
Beach Q is in such a bay; Beach P is on an open coast.
So Beach Q should usually have the bigger tidal range.

mistakes.A: Trap: guessing from size. The passage says funnel-shaped bays squeeze the water higher.
mistakes.B: Trap: ignoring a factor. The passage says 'the shape of the coast matters as well'.
mistakes.D: Trap: going too far. Squeezed water rises higher, but it still falls again.

questions.prompt: Passage C is written in free verse. This means the poem

options.A: has no line breaks
options.B: can be read without paying
options.C: must always be read aloud quickly
options.D: does not follow a regular pattern of rhyme or rhythm

questions.explanation: Free verse means poetry without a fixed rhyme scheme or regular beat — like this poem, whose lines vary in length and mostly do not rhyme. It still uses lines and stanzas.
steps: Check the poem: lines are different lengths and there is no regular rhyme.
'Free' means free from fixed patterns of rhyme and rhythm.
So free verse does not follow a regular rhyme or rhythm pattern.

mistakes.A: Trap: confusing free verse with prose. The poem is still set out in lines and stanzas.
mistakes.B: Trap: reading 'free' literally. In poetry, 'free' means free of fixed rules.
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a rule. Free verse has nothing to do with reading speed.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, what has most likely happened to the grandfather?

options.A: He is outside checking the weather and will be back soon.
options.B: He has moved his shed to a new house.
options.C: He is no longer alive, and the speaker misses him.
options.D: He has given up woodwork because he lost his glasses.

questions.explanation: The poem uses past tense for him ('never threw anything away', 'would say'), the bench is 'bare' and the glasses are 'waiting' — he will not return. 'As if he has just stepped out' tells us he hasn't really.
steps: Notice the tense: 'He never threw anything away', 'he would say' — things he used to do.
The glasses are 'waiting' and it is only 'as if' he stepped out — he is not coming back.
So the grandfather has most likely died, and the speaker misses him.

mistakes.A: Trap: taking 'as if' literally. 'As if he has just stepped out' means it only seems that way.
mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a detail. The speaker is standing in his shed.
mistakes.D: Trap: misusing a detail. His glasses are right there on the bench.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, the labels are written in ink 'gone brown as tea'. This tells us the labels are

options.A: written using tea instead of ink
options.B: wet and hard to read
options.C: old, written a long time ago
options.D: new and freshly written

questions.explanation: Ink fades and browns over many years, so ink 'gone brown as tea' shows the labels are old. The word 'gone' tells us the ink has changed, not that tea was used.
steps: 'Gone brown' means the ink has changed colour over time.
Ink fades to brown only after many years.
So the labels are old.

mistakes.A: Trap: reading the comparison literally. The ink has turned the colour of tea; it is still ink.
mistakes.B: Trap: picturing liquid. The comparison is only about colour.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing why ink changes colour. Ink fades to brown with age.

questions.prompt: Which line from Passage C contains personification?

options.A: "the ink gone brown as tea."
options.B: "folded, waiting,"
options.C: "Jars of screws line the shelves,"
options.D: "He never threw anything away."

questions.explanation: Glasses cannot wait; giving them this human action is personification — they seem to wait for their owner. 'Brown as tea' is a simile, not personification.
steps: Personification gives a human action or feeling to a non-human thing.
In 'folded, waiting', the reading glasses are 'waiting' like a person.
So 'folded, waiting' contains personification.

mistakes.A: Trap: naming a simile. This compares using 'as'; it does not give a human quality.
mistakes.C: Trap: a plain description. To 'line' shelves is an ordinary verb for things placed in a row.
mistakes.D: Trap: a literal statement about a person. Personification gives human qualities to things that are NOT human.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, why does the speaker put the jar back 'exactly where it was'?

options.A: To respect and keep the grandfather's order, as a way of holding on to him
options.B: Because the screws are too rusty to be useful
options.C: Because the speaker is afraid of getting in trouble
options.D: Because the speaker plans to sell everything in the shed and wants it to look neat for buyers

questions.explanation: The grandfather had 'a system only he understood'; returning the jar exactly keeps his system untouched, a sign of love and grief. Fear of trouble doesn't fit because he is no longer there.
steps: Remember the shelves follow 'a system only he understood'.
Putting the jar back 'exactly' keeps his system just as he left it.
So the speaker does it to respect his order and hold on to his memory.

mistakes.B: Trap: inventing a reason. Nothing says the screws are rusty.
mistakes.C: Trap: a reason that doesn't fit. The grandfather is gone, so no one will tell the speaker off.
mistakes.D: Trap: the opposite feeling. Someone planning to sell would not carefully return the jar.

questions.prompt: Which phrase best describes the overall mood of Passage C?

options.A: Angry and bitter
options.B: Spooky and frightening
options.C: Tender and sad
options.D: Cheerful and comic

questions.explanation: Loving details (careful capitals, the glasses) and the empty bench give a tender, sad mood. The 'applause' image is light, but it sits inside a poem about loss.
steps: Look at the details: careful labels, his sayings, the bare bench, the waiting glasses.
They are described lovingly, but they remind the speaker he is gone.
So the mood is tender and sad.

mistakes.A: Trap: no evidence. The speaker is gentle with every object.
mistakes.B: Trap: misreading the empty bench and 'waiting' glasses. They make us sad, not scared.
mistakes.D: Trap: picking out one image. 'Small applause' is gentle, but the poem is about missing someone.

questions.prompt: In Passage C, the grandfather kept 'a key to a lock that no longer existed'. Why does the poet include this item?

options.A: It shows he kept things after they had lost their use, and quietly hints at the loss in the poem.
options.B: It proves the grandfather was becoming forgetful and confused, keeping things without knowing what they were for.
options.C: It suggests the shed hides a secret locked room.
options.D: It shows the grandfather worked as a locksmith.

questions.explanation: A key with no lock is useless, yet he kept it — like the other odd items. It also echoes the poem's sadness: something that remains after what it belonged to is gone, like his glasses without him. 'Forgetful' contradicts his careful system.
steps: Note the list: a bent hinge, a single glove, a key with no lock — all things that have lost their use.
He kept them on purpose ('That might be useful'), showing his character.
Like the glasses without their owner, the key hints at loss — so it shows his habit and quietly echoes the poem's grief.

mistakes.B: Trap: judging him harshly. He kept things on purpose: 'That might be useful.'
mistakes.C: Trap: inventing a mystery. The lock 'no longer existed', so there is nothing to open.
mistakes.D: Trap: turning one object into a job. The other items (a hinge, a glove) are ordinary odds and ends.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the poster in Passage D?

options.A: To sell sausages at the reserve
options.B: To encourage local people to come and plant trees at the creek
options.C: To report on a planting day that has already happened
options.D: To teach people how to grow trees at home

questions.explanation: The headline, the time, the meeting place and the list of what to bring all invite people to the planting day. The sausage sizzle is just an extra reward.
steps: Look at the biggest text and the details: a headline about trees, then when and where to meet.
These invite readers to come along.
So the purpose is to encourage locals to come and plant trees.

mistakes.A: Trap: choosing the bonus. The sausage sizzle is free and in a corner; it is not the poster's purpose.
mistakes.C: Trap: misreading the photos. The poster gives a coming date, time and meeting place.
mistakes.D: Trap: choosing a minor line. 'We'll show you how' is about the planting day, not gardening at home.

questions.prompt: In Passage D, what do the two photographs and the white arrow suggest?

options.A: The planting day can change the creek from bare to green.
options.B: The creek used to be green and has now been damaged.
options.C: Two different creeks are being compared.
options.D: Trees can grow fully in a single morning.

questions.explanation: The arrow points from the bare bank to the same bank covered in trees, showing the change the planting can bring. Reading it the other way reverses the arrow.
steps: Note the order: bare bank on the left, green bank on the right.
The arrow points left to right — from bare to green — and it is 'the same creek bank'.
So the images suggest the planting day can turn the bare creek green.

mistakes.B: Trap: reading the arrow backwards. It points from the bare photo to the green one.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing a key word. The description says it is 'the same creek bank'.
mistakes.D: Trap: taking the image too literally. The photos show the hoped-for result, not a claim about growth speed.

questions.prompt: The headline in Passage D, 'ONE MORNING. ONE HUNDRED TREES. ONE CREEK REBORN.', mainly works by

options.A: asking the reader a question
options.B: giving statistics from scientific research about how many trees a creek needs
options.C: quoting an expert on creeks
options.D: repeating 'one' in short phrases so the goal sounds simple and achievable

questions.explanation: Three short phrases each start with 'one', building a rhythm and making a big change sound easy — just one morning. 'One hundred trees' is a target, not a research statistic.
steps: Spot the pattern: each phrase begins with 'ONE'.
The phrases are short and punchy, like a list of three.
This repetition makes the goal sound simple and achievable.

mistakes.A: Trap: naming a device that isn't there. There is no question mark.
mistakes.B: Trap: over-reading the number. 'One hundred trees' is a goal, not research data.
mistakes.C: Trap: naming a device that isn't there. There are no quotation marks or names.

questions.prompt: In the headline of Passage D, the word 'REBORN' means

options.A: born for the very first time
options.B: brought back to healthy life
options.C: moved to a new place
options.D: flooded with water again

questions.explanation: 'Re-' means again: the bare creek comes alive again with trees, as the right-hand photo shows. 'Born for the first time' ignores 're-'.
steps: Break the word: 're-' (again) + 'born'.
The photos show a bare creek becoming green.
So 'reborn' means brought back to healthy life.

mistakes.A: Trap: ignoring the prefix. 're-' means 'again', so it isn't the first time.
mistakes.C: Trap: guessing. The creek stays in the same place; the photos show the same bank.
mistakes.D: Trap: thinking about water. The photos show trees growing back, not flooding.

questions.prompt: Why is the sausage sizzle message in Passage D placed inside a tilted, bright yellow circle?

options.A: Because it is the most important information about when and where to meet
options.B: To show that it is a safety warning
options.C: Because it was added later by mistake
options.D: To make an extra reward stand out and catch the reader's eye

questions.explanation: A bright, tilted shape breaks the pattern and draws the eye to a bonus that may persuade people to come. The key details (time, place) are elsewhere, so it isn't the most important information.
steps: Notice the design: bright yellow, a circle, tilted — different from the rest.
The message is a reward: a free sausage sizzle.
So it is designed to make the extra reward stand out and attract readers.

mistakes.A: Trap: mixing up the bonus and the details. The time and meeting place are in the black writing.
mistakes.B: Trap: confusing colours. Yellow is bright, but the message is a treat, not a warning.
mistakes.C: Trap: guessing. Designers tilt and colour things on purpose to grab attention.

questions.prompt: A parent who has never planted a tree wants to bring her eight-year-old to the event in Passage D. Which statement does the poster support?

options.A: They must book at the library front desk first, or they will be turned away on the day.
options.B: They can come: children are welcome with an adult and no experience is needed.
options.C: They must bring their own gloves and tools.
options.D: The child cannot come because the event is for adults only.

questions.explanation: Two bullet points cover both worries: 'Children welcome with an adult' and 'No experience needed'. The small print says bookings are not essential, so they will not be turned away.
steps: Check the bullet points: 'Children welcome with an adult' and 'No experience needed'.
Check the small print: bookings are 'not essential'.
So they can come, even without experience or a booking.

mistakes.A: Trap: misreading the small print. It says bookings are 'not essential'.
mistakes.C: Trap: missing a bullet point. Gloves and tools are provided.
mistakes.D: Trap: missing a bullet point. 'Children welcome with an adult.'

questions.prompt: Why does the poster in Passage D say that bookings 'help us order enough trees'?

options.A: To warn that the whole event will be cancelled if not enough people book in advance
options.B: To give people a practical reason to book even though booking is not required
options.C: To show that only one hundred people can come
options.D: To explain that each planter must buy their own tree

questions.explanation: Bookings are 'not essential', so the organisers explain why booking still helps — it lets them order the right number of trees. Nothing suggests the event will be cancelled.
steps: Read the whole line: bookings are 'not essential, but they help us order enough trees.'
'But' introduces a reason to book anyway.
So it gives a practical reason to book, even though booking isn't required.

mistakes.A: Trap: overstating. Nothing says the event might be cancelled.
mistakes.C: Trap: mixing up numbers. One hundred is the number of trees, not a limit on people.
mistakes.D: Trap: misreading 'order'. The organisers order the trees; planters are not asked to pay.
